title.en: Vary buildings by what happens inside them

summary: Differentiate structures by their program, materials and site rather than by random size and rotation jitter.
objective: Turn a repeated-house village into a settlement whose silhouette carries information about work, wealth and terrain.
applies_when: A scene contains several buildings, tents, workshops or stalls of the same family.
A village, market, camp or town block looks repetitive or uniformly random.
The brief asks for a place with a story, an economy or a history.
intent_signals: the houses all look the same
make the village feel lived in
add a smithy and a mill
example_prompts: Give the village a mill, a smithy and a granary that read differently from a distance.
Make the harbour buildings look like they belong to the harbour.
negative_signals: Deliberately uniform architecture such as barracks, container yards or planned identical housing, where sameness is the subject.
Background scenery too far away to resolve any of these features.
not_for: Deliberately uniform architecture such as barracks, container yards or planned identical housing, where sameness is the subject.
Background scenery too far away to resolve any of these features.

principles: Random jitter of one prototype produces variety without meaning: the eye reads noise, not a settlement. Function produces silhouettes that differ in ways a viewer can name.

Programs impose consequences on shape once you have chosen how the world works. If your mill is water driven it needs a wheel and access to the water; a smithy that burns fuel needs a flue and a working yard; a store built to keep grain dry needs whatever your setting uses for that, whether a raised floor, a sealed jar or a cold cellar. These are motifs that follow from a chosen process, not universal requirements of every mill or granary.
Site and material continue the story: the same program in stone, timber or mud brick differs in wall thickness, opening size and roof pitch, and slope forces terraces, stilts or split levels.
implementation: List three to six programs for the settlement and give each one distinguishing feature that survives at the intended viewing distance: roof shape, chimney, opening pattern, attached yard or projecting structure.
Derive secondary detail from the program rather than adding it uniformly: fuel and tools at the smithy, sacks and a hoist at the granary, drying racks at the fishery.

Let the site sort the buildings: workshops near power or water, storage near the route out, dwellings filling the space between, and orient ridge lines to the slope or prevailing wind you have chosen.
Keep a shared vocabulary of joinery, roof material and colour so the differences read as one culture rather than as a sample sheet.
observable_checks: Render a distant silhouette pass: if three named buildings cannot be identified from the outline alone, the variation is decorative.
Ask what each building consumes and produces; a building with no answer is filler and can be merged or removed.
Look for the tell of jitter: identical footprints at different angles, or scaled copies whose door heights no longer match the ground.
Check that special structures sit where their function needs them, not where they happened to be scattered.

creative_affordances: Invented economies and fictional crafts work as well as historical ones; the rule asks for consequences, not authenticity.
Stylised exaggeration of a functional feature, such as an oversized wheel or chimney, is a legitimate way to make the program readable.
known_limits: Authored creative guidance; it makes no claim about the actual construction practice of any real place or period.
Historical or heritage subjects need separate evidence work before a reconstruction is presented as such.
